content: Panthenol is the alcohol analog of pantothenic acid, also known as vitamin B5, and serves as the provitamin of B5. Within biological systems, it is rapidly oxidized to pantothenate. At room temperature, panthenol exists as a highly viscous, transparent liquid. In contrast, salts of pantothenic acid, such as sodium pantothenate, are typically white powders. Panthenol is highly soluble in water, alcohol, and propylene glycol. It is also soluble in ether and chloroform, while demonstrating slight solubility in glycerin. The compound exists in two enantiomeric forms: D-panthenol and L-panthenol. Only the D-form, also referred to as dexpanthenol, is biologically active. However, both enantiomers exhibit moisturizing properties. For cosmetic applications, panthenol is available either as the D-form or as a racemic mixture of Dand L-panthenol (DL-panthenol). The expanded chemical formula of panthenol is HO-CH2-C(CH3)2-CH(OH)-CONH-CH2CH2CH2-OH. In cosmetics, panthenol functions as a humectant, emollient, and moisturizer. It is often used in concentrations of 1-5%. When applied to hair, it coats the strands, seals their surface, and lubricates the follicles, resulting in a shiny appearance. In ointments, panthenol is frequently combined with allantoin in concentrations of 2-5% and is used to treat sunburns, mild burns, and minor skin disorders. It is important to note that panthenol is not absorbed through the skin, which limits its effects to those unrelated to its provitamin properties. When ingested, panthenol is metabolized into pantothenic acid.
